common_name: Bluetta Blueberry (Compact Early-Season Northern Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in acidic, well-drained soil in full sun; pairs well with other early-season highbush types for extended cross-pollination.

directions: Bluetta is a compact, medium-vigor northern highbush blueberry that ripens early, typically among the first highbush varieties to color up in June. Amend soil to a pH of 4.5-6.5 with pine bark or peat before planting, and mulch heavily to keep the shallow root system cool and moist. The dense, globe-shaped bush produces up to 10 pounds of sweet fruit at maturity and turns a attractive scarlet in fall, making it useful as a dual-purpose edible landscape shrub. Because it ripens early, it is a good choice for gardeners wanting to start the blueberry harvest season as soon as possible.

common_name: Hannah's Choice Blueberry (Early-Ripening USDA/NJAES Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil; ripens about two days ahead of 'Duke', so pair with another early cultivar for cross-pollination.

directions: Hannah's Choice is a tetraploid highbush blueberry developed through the joint USDA Agricultural Research Service and New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station breeding program, selected for improved sweetness and firmness over other early cultivars. The medium-to-large, light-to-medium blue berries have a notably sweet, sub-acid flavor with distinct peach-like accents, and mature plants can yield 8-15 pounds of fruit per bush. Grow in well-drained, highly acidic soil with a thick mulch layer and consistent moisture, since highbush blueberries have shallow fibrous roots that dry out quickly.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Blue Suede Blueberry (UGA Low-Chill Southern Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Set out dormant bushes in fall or winter in acidic soil; needs only 500-550 chill hours, making it a strong fit for Gulf South winters.

directions: Blue Suede is a University of Georgia southern highbush release (bred by D. Scott NeSmith and Mark Ehlenfeldt, trialed as TH-682) bred for low-chill climates, needing only about 500-550 hours below 45°F — well suited to mild Gulf Coast winters. The vigorous plant produces an abundance of large, flavorful, light-blue berries over a protracted mid-season ripening window, giving home gardeners a longer picking period than many single-flush cultivars. It is also an attractive landscape shrub, with showy spring flowers and deep red fall foliage. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil with a thick organic mulch and pair with another low-chill southern highbush cultivar for best fruit set.
sources: University of Georgia College of Agricultural and Environmental Sciences

common_name: Earliblue Blueberry (Classic Very-Early Northern Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil; one of the earliest-ripening highbush cultivars, useful for extending the start of harvest season.

directions: Earliblue was released in 1952 by the cooperative USDA and New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station breeding program as a cross of 'Stanley' and 'Weymouth', combining both parents' very early ripening with firmer fruit than Weymouth alone. It remains one of the earliest-maturing highbush blueberries grown, producing medium-to-large, light blue, firm berries with good flavor well ahead of midseason varieties. Give it very acidic, well-drained soil (pH 4.5-5.2) amended with pine bark or peat, and mulch heavily since highbush blueberries have shallow roots that dry out quickly in summer heat.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Stanley Blueberry (Historic High-Flavor Heirloom Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil; ripens midseason, late July to early August in most of its range.

directions: Stanley is a historic heirloom highbush blueberry selected by USDA breeder Frederick Coville in 1921 from a cross of 'Katharine' and a wild Rubel bush. It is widely regarded as one of the most flavorful blueberries ever introduced, with firm, aromatic, sweet-subacid berries of exceptionally high dessert quality, ripening midseason in a mature bush that can yield 8-12 pounds of fruit. Grow in very acidic, well-drained soil with a thick mulch layer, and prune out the oldest canes each winter to keep the bush productive, since it is an older selection that benefits from regular renewal pruning more than some modern cultivars.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil; ripens early to midseason with a small, dry picking scar that resists rot in storage.

directions: Collins was released in 1959 and remains valued for its vigorous, productive, semi-upright growth habit and large, light blue, crack-resistant berries with good flavor. Its small, dry picking scar means ripe fruit holds on the bush well without dropping and stores better than many older varieties. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat, keep consistently moist with mulch, and prune annually to renew fruiting wood and keep the upright canes from becoming overly dense.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Herbert Blueberry (Large-Fruited High-Flavor Heirloom Highbush Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil; spreading habit benefits from extra spacing and annual pruning to keep fruit easy to reach.

directions: Herbert was developed in 1932 and introduced in 1953, and is still prized by home growers for its exceptionally large, tender berries with rich, aromatic flavor that many describe as reminiscent of wild mountain huckleberries. The plant has a notably spreading growth habit, so give it extra room compared to more upright cultivars, and stake or prune to keep heavily laden branches from sprawling onto the ground. Plant in very acidic, well-drained soil with a thick mulch layer, and because the fruit is soft and tender, pick promptly at full ripeness for best fresh-eating quality.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Plant in acidic, well-drained soil; valued mainly for very early ripening and as a breeding parent rather than fresh-market fruit quality.

directions: Weymouth is one of the oldest named highbush blueberry selections, grown mainly for its very early ripening rather than top dessert quality — the dark blue berries are soft and mildly flavored, and can drop from the bush if left unpicked too long. It served as a key early-ripening parent in the breeding of later cultivars such as 'Earliblue'. Needs insect pollinators for good fruit set and is largely resistant to common blueberry diseases apart from Phomopsis canker. Grow in acidic, well-drained soil like other highbush types, and treat it more as a historical or collector's planting than a top fresh-eating choice given newer, better-flavored early cultivars now available.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station
